summary: Defines additional RADIUS attributes for IEEE 802 networks and clarifies how the EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id attributes are used. It updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072.

plainLanguage.summary: When a laptop joins a Wi-Fi network, the access point usually asks a central server whether to let it in. This RFC adds the extra pieces of information that server and access point can exchange: which networks the user may use, the name of the session, the cipher suites the radio used, and the name of the building the hotspot is in.

subtitle: New RADIUS attributes that let Wi-Fi and wired access points tell a central server more and get more back.

tldr.problem: RFC 3580 already set out how RADIUS should be used inside IEEE 802 networks, but an access point had few ways to tell the RADIUS server about the details of a login, and few ways to get some of those details back.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines a set of new RADIUS attributes that carry the allowed networks, the EAP session identifier, venue details and the cipher suites in use, and it clarifies how the EAP-Key-Name and Called-Station-Id attributes must be used.
tldr.outcome: The result is a RADIUS server that can make access decisions with more context and can return the key material a client needs for MACsec. RFC 7268 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072 and was later updated by RFC 8044.

today: RFC 7268 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072. It was later updated by RFC 8044 and has not been obsoleted, so the attribute numbers it assigned are still the ones in use for IEEE 802 RADIUS deployments.

sections.title: Why More RADIUS Attributes
sections.content:
When an organization wants to manage authentication, authorization and accounting (AAA) centrally for IEEE 802 networks, it deploys a backend authentication and accounting server, and the IEEE 802 authenticators act as AAA clients for it. RADIUS is the protocol they use.

RFC 3580 already provides guidelines for using RADIUS within IEEE 802 local area networks. This RFC adds to that: it defines additional attributes suitable for use by IEEE 802 authenticators acting as AAA clients, and it clarifies the usage of two attributes that already existed, the EAP-Key-Name Attribute and the Called-Station-Id Attribute. It updates RFC 3580 and RFC 4072.

Most of the document is a reference list. Each new attribute gets a description, a packet format, the type number it was assigned, and the rules for when it may and may not appear. The attributes fall into a few families: ones that restrict where a user may connect, ones that carry names and identifiers from the Extensible Authentication Protocol (EAP), and ones that describe the wireless network itself.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC is mostly a catalogue. For each new piece of information it gives a format, a number, and the rule for when to send it.

sections.title: The Parts of an 802 Login
sections.content:
Section 1.1 defines the words the rest of the document uses.

An Access Point (AP) is a station that provides access to the distribution services over the wireless medium for associated stations. A Station (STA) is any device with an IEEE 802.11 conformant Medium Access Control (MAC) and Physical Layer interface to the wireless medium. Association is the service used to establish the AP-to-station mapping and enable the station to use the distribution system services.

An Authenticator is the entity that requires authentication from the Supplicant; it may be connected to the Supplicant at the other end of a point-to-point LAN segment or wireless link. The Supplicant is the entity being authenticated by the authenticator. The Authentication Server is the entity that provides the authentication service to the authenticator, verifying the claim of identity made by the Supplicant using the credentials the Supplicant provides.

These roles come from the IEEE 802 standards themselves, not from this RFC. The RFC uses them to say which packet each attribute may travel in.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC names the four roles in a network login: the device trying to get in, the device asking it to prove itself, the server that checks the proof, and the wireless link they share.

sections.title: Allowed-Called-Station-Id
sections.content:
The Allowed-Called-Station-Id Attribute, type 174, lets the RADIUS server name the authenticator MAC addresses and networks that the user is allowed to connect to. One or more of these attributes may be included in an Access-Accept, a CoA-Request or an Accounting-Request packet. If the Called-Station-Id the user actually connects to does not match one of them, the Network Access Server (NAS) MUST NOT permit the user to access the network.

It is designed for pre-authentication. In IEEE 802.11 pre-authentication, a Called-Station-Id Attribute is typically not included in the Access-Request, so the RADIUS server does not know which network the user is trying to reach. Allowed-Called-Station-Id lets the server restrict the networks and attachment points the user may connect to afterwards.

For IEEE 802 the attribute holds the Medium Access Control (MAC) address as an uppercase ASCII character string in Canonical format, with octet values separated by a hyphen, for example 00-10-A4-23-19-C0. Where restrictions on both the network and the authenticator MAC address are wanted, the network name must be appended after a colon, for example 00-10-A4-23-19-C0:AP1. Where no MAC address restriction is wanted, the MAC address field must be omitted but the colon and the network name must still be there, for example :AP1.

The network name is the Service Set Identifier (SSID) within IEEE 802.11, and the Network-Id Name (NID-Name) within IEEE 802.1X wired networks. Because a NID-Name can be up to 253 octets, there may not be room in the attribute for both a MAC address and a network name when 802.1X wired networks are used. The RFC does not consider that serious, because the attribute is expected to be used largely in wireless access scenarios.
sections.plainLanguage: This attribute is the list of places a user may connect to. The server sends the list back with the access decision, and the access point refuses the user if the network they landed on is not on that list.

sections.title: EAP-Key-Name and the MACsec Key
sections.content:
The EAP-Key-Name Attribute, type 102 as assigned in RFC 4072, carries the EAP Session-Id as described in the EAP Key Management Framework of RFC 5247. How the attribute is used depends on the link layer in question, and not all link layers use the name at all. It may be included in Access-Request, Access-Accept and CoA-Request packets.

The NAS operates as a pass-through in EAP, so it cannot know the EAP Session-Id before the RADIUS server sends it. That produces a set of rules. An EAP-Key-Name Attribute sent in an Access-Request MUST contain only a single NUL character. A RADIUS server that receives an Access-Request with an EAP-Key-Name Attribute containing anything other than a single NUL character MUST silently discard the attribute. The server SHOULD include the attribute in an Access-Accept or a CoA-Request only if one was present in the Access-Request. If it was present in the request but not in the Access-Accept, the NAS SHOULD treat the Access-Accept as though it were an Access-Reject. If it was not present in the request but is present in the Access-Accept, the NAS SHOULD silently discard it.

Why this matters is MACsec. As described in Section 6.2.2 of IEEE 802.1X, the Connectivity Association Key Name (CKN) is derived from the EAP Session-Id, and the CKN is then used in the derivation of the Key Encrypting Key (KEK) and the Integrity Check Value Key (ICK), which protect the Secure Association Keys used by Media Access Control Security. For the NAS to acquire the information it needs for the MACsec Key Agreement exchange, it has to include the EAP-Key-Name Attribute in the Access-Request and receive it back from the RADIUS server in the Access-Accept.
sections.plainLanguage: The session name cannot travel from the client to the server, because the access point does not know it either. So the client sends an empty placeholder and the server fills in the real name on the way back. Wired networks use that name to derive the keys that protect their traffic.

sections.title: EAP-Peer-Id and EAP-Server-Id
sections.content:
The EAP-Peer-Id Attribute, type 175, carries a Peer-Id generated by the EAP method, and the EAP-Server-Id Attribute, type 176, carries a Server-Id generated by the EAP method. Both have a length of at least 3 octets, and both are strings that a robust implementation SHOULD support as undistinguished octets. How each name is used depends on the link layer in question, and the RFC notes that not all link layers use these names and that existing EAP method implementations do not generate them.

Both attributes follow the same pass-through rules as EAP-Key-Name. The EAP-Peer-Id Attribute may be included in Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request packets, but more than one MUST NOT be included in an Access-Request, while one or more may be included in an Access-Accept. An EAP-Peer-Id Attribute sent in an Access-Request MUST only contain a single NUL character; a home RADIUS server that receives anything else in it MUST silently discard the attribute; the server SHOULD include one or more EAP-Peer-Id Attributes in an Access-Accept only if one was present in the Access-Request; and a NAS that receives them in an Access-Accept without having included one in the Access-Request SHOULD silently discard them. Only a single EAP Peer-Id may be included per attribute.

The EAP-Server-Id Attribute is only allowed in Access-Request, Access-Accept and Accounting-Request packets. More than one MUST NOT be included in an Access-Request, while one or more may be included in an Access-Accept. The same single NUL rule applies to an EAP-Server-Id Attribute sent in an Access-Request, and a home RADIUS server that receives anything other than a single NUL character MUST silently discard it. The server SHOULD include it in an Access-Accept only if one was present in the Access-Request.
sections.plainLanguage: These two attributes hold names that the EAP method may produce. They follow the same rule as the session name: an empty placeholder goes out to the server, and the real name comes back.

sections.title: Identifiers, Timers and Announcements
sections.content:
The next group of attributes carries small values, mostly in a four-octet field where the two most significant octets are set to zero by the sender and ignored by the receiver.

The Mobility-Domain-Id Attribute, type 177, lets the NAS give the RADIUS server the Mobility Domain Identifier defined in Section 8.4.2.49 of IEEE 802.11. Its value is a 32-bit unsigned integer whose two least significant octets carry the identifier. The Preauth-Timeout Attribute, type 178, is a 32-bit unsigned integer giving the maximum number of seconds that pre-authentication state must be kept by the NAS without being used. For example, when IEEE 802.11 pre-authentication is used and the user has not used the Pairwise Master Key derived from it within that time, the access point MAY discard the key. Once the session is underway the attribute has no bearing on the maximum session time, which is set by the Session-Timeout Attribute instead.

The Network-Id-Name Attribute, type 179, carries the NID-Name used by IEEE 802.1X implementations. It may be up to 253 octets long, where the IEEE 802.11 SSID is at most 32 octets, so the RFC says the Called-Station-Id Attribute SHOULD contain only the MAC address when used with IEEE 802.1X, and the Network-Id-Name Attribute carries the name. The attribute MUST NOT be used to encode the IEEE 802.11 SSID. Zero or one may be present in an Access-Request, Access-Challenge, Access-Accept or Accounting-Request; in an Access-Request it is a hint of the NID-Name the Supplicant should be granted access to, in an Access-Accept it is the NID-Name to which access is to be granted, and in an Accounting-Request it is the NID-Name to which access has been granted.

The EAPoL-Announcement Attribute, type 180, carries EAPoL-Announcement Type-Length-Value tuples as defined in IEEE 802.1X. EAPoL stands for Extensible Authentication Protocol over Local Area Network. Zero or more may appear in an Access-Request, Access-Accept, Access-Challenge, Access-Reject, Accounting-Request, CoA-Request or Disconnect-Request. In an Access-Request the attribute carries the announcements the user sent; in the other packets it carries what the NAS is to send to the user in a unicast EAPoL-Announcement; in an Accounting-Request it carries what the NAS most recently sent. Because RADIUS attributes are short, the String fields of several EAPoL-Announcement Attributes MUST be concatenated before the tuples are parsed, and any tuple longer than 253 octets MUST be fragmented across several attributes.
sections.plainLanguage: These attributes carry the small facts a server needs about a network: which mobility domain it belongs to, how long a pre-login may be kept, the name of the wired network, and any announcement the client made during the login.

sections.title: Which Attributes Go in Which Packet
sections.content:
Section 3 of the RFC is a table showing, for every attribute, how many copies may appear in each kind of RADIUS packet. Three notations are used. A zero means the attribute MUST NOT be present in that packet. Zero or more means any number of instances MAY be present. Zero or one means a single instance MAY be present.

The table makes the intended direction of travel clear. WLAN-Reason-Code, which says why access was refused, may appear only in an Access-Reject or a Disconnect-Request. Allowed-Called-Station-Id appears in none of the four Access packets but may appear any number of times in an Access-Accept, a CoA-Request or an Accounting-Request. EAPoL-Announcement is the only attribute that may appear in all four Access packets.

Section 4 records the IANA side. The document uses the RADIUS namespace, and type numbers were assigned for the new attributes: Allowed-Called-Station-Id 174, EAP-Peer-Id 175, EAP-Server-Id 176, Mobility-Domain-Id 177, Preauth-Timeout 178, Network-Id-Name 179, EAPoL-Announcement 180, WLAN-HESSID 181, WLAN-Venue-Info 182, WLAN-Venue-Language 183, WLAN-Venue-Name 184, WLAN-Reason-Code 185, WLAN-Pairwise-Cipher 186, WLAN-Group-Cipher 187, WLAN-AKM-Suite 188, WLAN-Group-Mgmt-Cipher 189, and WLAN-RF-Band 190. Because the specification relies entirely on values assigned by IEEE 802, no registries are established for maintenance by the IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: The table is a delivery instruction sheet: it says which pieces of information may travel in which kind of message, and how many copies are allowed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because this document describes the use of RADIUS for authentication, authorization and accounting in IEEE 802 networks, it is vulnerable to all of the threats that are present in other RADIUS applications. The RFC points at RFC 2607, RFC 2865, RFC 3162, RFC 3579, RFC 3580 and RFC 5176 for a discussion of those threats.

One point is called out directly. When RADIUS traffic is sent in the clear, the attributes defined in this document can be obtained by an attacker snooping the exchange between the RADIUS client and server. RADIUS confidentiality is therefore desirable, and the RFC refers to RFC 6421 for a review of RADIUS security and crypto-agility requirements.

The RFC also discusses using the WLAN attributes to make access decisions. A RADIUS server can decide whether to accept or reject an Access-Request based on the values of the WLAN-Pairwise-Cipher, WLAN-Group-Cipher, WLAN-AKM-Suite, WLAN-Group-Mgmt-Cipher and WLAN-RF-Band attributes, but the value of doing so is limited. In general an Access-Reject should not be necessary, except where access points and stations are misconfigured so as to enable connections with unacceptable values, and in that case users would be better served by fixing the misconfiguration than by having their access rejected on an ongoing basis.

Where access does need to be rejected, the user should be given a reason. If the WLAN-Pairwise-Cipher, WLAN-Group-Cipher, WLAN-AKM-Suite or WLAN-Group-Mgmt-Cipher values in the Access-Request are not acceptable to the RADIUS server, then a WLAN-Reason-Code Attribute with a value of 29, requested service rejected because of service provider ciphersuite or AKM requirement, SHOULD be returned in the Access-Reject. If the WLAN-RF-Band value is not acceptable, then a WLAN-Reason-Code Attribute with a value of 11, disassociated because the information in the Supported Channels element is unacceptable, SHOULD be returned in the Access-Reject.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending RADIUS traffic in the clear exposes everything in these attributes to anyone watching the exchange. The RFC also says that rejecting a user for using a weak cipher is usually the wrong fix: the access point should be reconfigured instead.
